question: How do Morgan Stanley, Merrill and Raymond James each approach advisor recruiting and retention?

claims.text: Morgan Stanley: The firm recruits financial advisors through its advisor-led channel, while also receiving flows into that channel from its workplace funnel.

Morgan Stanley: The firm attributes advisor recruiting interest to the platform it has invested in: "There's obviously a great platform. We have recruits that are interested in what we've been investing in."
Morgan Stanley: Per a 1Q25 transcript, advisor recruitment remains strong, which the firm attributes to its reputation as an exceptional place where financial advisors can grow their businesses.

Morgan Stanley: Per a 1Q25 transcript, the firm attracts advisors by offering unique access to intellectual capital, world-class technology and compensation viewed as fair and motivating, and it is selective about recruiting.

Morgan Stanley: Per the 2Q25 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2025), the firm grants employee loans under a program established primarily to recruit certain Wealth Management financial advisors; these loans are full recourse, generally require periodic repayments, and are due in full upon termination of employment.

Merrill: Per a 4Q25 Bank of America transcript, Merrill is picking up the recruiting of experienced advisors, but this is not an enormous part of its strategy; its core approach is a training program that trains people in wealth management at Bank of America and Merrill, which the firm believes drives net new flows.

Merrill: Per a 2Q25 Bank of America transcript, Merrill adds financial advisors to the sales force in Merrill and the Private Bank through its extensive training program and experienced hiring of advisors.

Merrill: Per its web page as of 2026-11-03, the Advisor Development Program is a multi-role training path (Client Associate, Financial Solutions Advisor, Financial Advisor, Core Advisor) through which candidates obtain the SIE, Series 7 and Series 66 licenses and progress to become a Merrill Financial Advisor, with each stage lasting roughly 13 months to 1-4 years.

Merrill: Per its web page as of 2026-11-03, as part of its Advisor Development Program recruiting pitch the firm offers industry-leading training and dedicated study time to obtain securities licenses, opportunities for existing advisors with Series 7 and 66, base salary and unlimited earning potential, high-quality leads and direct client interactions, and coaching and mentorship.

Merrill: Per a November 2026 trade press report, Merrill largely pulled back from veteran broker recruiting at the end of 2017 but returned to it after Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf (who took over in 2023) restored a focus on hiring and a more aggressive offer; recruited assets to the wealth unit doubled year-over-year as a result.

Merrill: Per a 1Q26 Bank of America transcript, the firm continues to attract talent across both new and experienced advisers, driving productivity higher on newer and existing members of the financial advisers team.

Merrill: Per a 2Q26 Bank of America transcript, Merrill and the Private Bank continue to attract talented advisers drawn to the breadth of the firm's platform and its ability to deliver comprehensive solutions for clients.

Raymond James: Per a 2Q26 transcript, the firm prefers to recruit financial advisors one-by-one rather than through acquisitions, because transition assistance fully goes to advisor retention and it lets the firm ensure cultural fit.

Raymond James: Per a 3Q26 transcript, the firm does not lead with the highest check; it seeks competitive economics but leads with culture and capabilities, offering a differentiated value proposition.
Raymond James: Per a 3Q26 transcript, the firm remains disciplined on transition assistance and the economics offered to advisors.

Raymond James: Per the fiscal 2025 10-K, the firm offers multiple affiliation options, referred to as AdvisorChoice, under which financial advisors affiliate as employees, independent contractors, or employees of third-party RIAs and broker-dealers.

Raymond James: Per the fiscal 2025 10-K, the firm participates, with limited exceptions, in the Protocol for Broker Recruiting, which governs the client information advisors may take and their ability to solicit clients when affiliating with a new firm.
Raymond James: Per the fiscal 2025 10-K, the firm offers loans to financial advisors for recruiting and retention purposes.
Raymond James: Per the fiscal 2025 10-K, cultural fit is a requirement for both the firm's recruiting and acquisition efforts.
Raymond James: Per the 2025 investor day deck, the firm's recruiting approach includes collaborative recruiting across channels, a West Coast and Northeast focus, and a next gen advisor strategy.

Raymond James: Per a 3Q26 transcript, the firm emphasizes consistency in recruiting, noting recruiting cannot be turned on and off quarter-to-quarter and requires a consistent value proposition and a team focused on finding advisors who are good cultural fits.

Raymond James: Per trade press (September 2026), the firm builds its advisory ranks through individualized recruitment rather than large-scale acquisitions, evaluating each prospective advisor on a one-on-one basis.
Raymond James: Per a 2Q26 transcript, the firm has broken out the cost of recruiting and retention to provide transparency on how much it pays to recruit and grow the firm.
Raymond James: Per a 3Q26 transcript, the firm's growth starts with keeping existing advisors satisfied and maintaining high retention of existing advisors.

Raymond James: Per a 3Q26 transcript, the firm's differentiated value proposition is that advisors do not have to choose between culture and capabilities, offering a combination of an advisor- and client-focused culture with leading technology, products and solutions.
Raymond James: Per the fiscal 2025 10-K, the firm has designed a compensation structure, including benefit plans and programs, intended to be attractive to current and prospective associates.

Raymond James: Per the fiscal 2025 10-K, the firm's ability to attract high quality advisors is based on its values-based culture, commitment to service, and the unique ways it provides services to financial advisors.

The three firms' recruiting and retention approaches differ in structure and emphasis, and the reported recruiting results are not directly comparable across firms. Morgan Stanley recruits through its advisor-led channel (with flows also coming from its workplace funnel) and emphasizes its platform, intellectual capital and technology, with retention built on deferred compensation (75% cash / 25% stock) and a >99% adviser retention rate rather than retention bonuses. Merrill anchors its strategy on an internal training (Advisor Development) program while also selectively ramping veteran/experienced advisor recruiting since 2023, with retention through training, leads, mentorship and platform tools, and near-historic-low adviser attrition. Raymond James recruits one-by-one (not via acquisitions), leads with culture and AdvisorChoice multiple affiliation options rather than the highest check, and reports quantified recruiting results (trailing 12-month production and client assets). The firms' respective recruiting results differ in definition and unit: Morgan Stanley reports net new assets and qualitative recruiting strength without a separate recruiting-specific figure; Merrill reports recruited assets (doubling year-over-year) and individual team wins; Raymond James reports trailing 12-month recruited production (e.g., $538 million in fiscal 2026) and client assets. Because these use different metrics, units and periods, they are not comparable head-to-head on a single number.
